structured_output.hypothesis: In measured cross-sectional median stature by age for US males, annual height velocity is highest in infancy, is lower and roughly constant across ages 4–9, rises to a clear peak in the early teens, and falls to near zero by ages 18–20.
structured_output.pass_criterion: Using survey-weighted median measured stature (recumbent length under 2 years) by single year of age for males 0–20, and annual velocity as the difference between successive age medians, ALL of the following hold. (a) Mean velocity for ages 0–1 is at least 2.0 times the mean velocity for ages 5–9. (b) For ages 4–9, velocity ranges within 2.0 cm/yr (max minus min) and every value is at least 4.0 cm/yr, so growth is slower but steady. (c) The maximum velocity at ages 10–16 is at least 1.25 times the mean velocity for ages 5–9, and the peak falls at age 11–15. (d) Mean velocity at ages 18–20 is below 1.0 cm/yr. Females are analysed the same way as a secondary check and do not affect the verdict.
structured_output.fail_criterion: The claim is refuted if any one of (a)–(d) fails for males. In particular, it fails if the maximum velocity at ages 10–16 is below 1.25 times the mean velocity for ages 5–9, which means no marked teen quickening. It also fails if velocity at ages 4–9 varies by more than 2.0 cm/yr, or if mean velocity at ages 18–20 is 1.0 cm/yr or more.
structured_output.interpretation: Thompson's 'curve of growth for length or stature' is read as the growth-velocity curve, that is, the derivative of height with respect to age. 'Rapid increase at the outset' is infancy (0–2 y). 'Long period of slower, but still rapid and almost steady growth in early boyhood' is ages about 4–9. 'Marked quickening in the teens' is the adolescent growth spurt. 'Gradual arrest' is the approach to adult height. Modern reinterpretation: a cross-sectional survey of many individuals stands in for longitudinal growth of one person. Age-median differences approximate individual velocity but blur the timing of the spurt, because individuals peak at different ages. The 2.0 cm/yr and 1.25× thresholds are set before any data are seen.

dataset.name: National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES) – Body Measures (Examination data)
dataset.publisher: US CDC National Center for Health Statistics (NCHS)
dataset.why_it_fits: NHANES records measured, not self-reported, standing height (BMXHT) and recumbent length for young children (BMXRECUM). It also records age in years and months (RIDAGEYR, RIDAGEMN), sex (RIAGENDR) and survey weights (WTMEC2YR) in the Demographics files. The data can be downloaded as SAS transport files with no registration. Together these cover ages 0–20 and allow weighted medians by age and sex.
